title: Dimensional Collapse in Transformer Attention Outputs: A Challenge for Sparse Dictionary Learning
abstract: Transformer architectures, and their attention mechanisms in particular, form the foundation of modern large language models. While transformer models are widely believed to operate in high-dimensional hidden spaces, we show that attention outputs are confined to a surprisingly low-dimensional subspace, with an effective dimensionality of only about 60\% of the full space---a phenomenon that is consistently observed across diverse model families and datasets, and arises from overlap among the output subspaces of different attention heads. Critically, we find this low-rank structure as a key factor of the prevalent dead feature problem in sparse dictionary learning, where it creates a mismatch between randomly initialized features and the intrinsic geometry of the activation space. Building on this insight, we propose a subspace-constrained training method for sparse autoencoders (SAEs), initializing feature directions into the active subspace of activations. Our approach reduces dead features from 87\% to below 1\% in Attention Output SAEs with 1M features, and can further extend to other sparse dictionary learning methods. Our findings provide both new insights into the geometry of attention and practical tools for improving sparse dictionary learning in large language models. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Llamascopium}.
problem: Sparse dictionary learning for transformer attention outputs fails due to the dead feature problem, where randomly initialized features mismatch the intrinsically low-dimensional geometry of attention subspaces.
approach: Subspace-constrained training for sparse autoencoders that initializes feature directions into the active subspace of attention activations, leveraging the observation that attention outputs are confined to 60% of the full dimensional space.
contribution: Reduces dead features from 87% to below 1% in 1M-feature Attention Output SAEs and demonstrates the approach extends to other sparse dictionary learning methods.
